## Why the classified 6,000 pages stay classified

[John Kiriakou](/wiki/john-kiriakou) said on Live on the Fly in November 2021 that the full 6,000-page [Senate Torture Report](/wiki/senate-torture-report) has remained classified — with only the executive summary released — for the reason the classification system is used everywhere in Washington: not to protect a genuine national-security secret but *"to avoid embarrassment"* over conduct that would expose *"domestic crime and international crime."* *"Every page of that,"* he said, *"I would imagine reveals that, and that's why it's classified."*<Cite t="49:18" /><Cite t="50:22" />

john-kiriakou.body_append:
## William Florence at Kiriakou's trial

[John Kiriakou](/wiki/john-kiriakou) has said that at his 2013 trial his defence called as a witness William Florence — a Pentagon official who had just retired after a thirty-year career writing most of the Defense Department's classification regulations. Florence, on Kiriakou's account, delivered the same testimony under oath at the trial that he had already given to the Congressional Government Information Committee: only about *"5 percent of the information that was classified deserved classification at the time it was classified,"* falling to *"one-tenth of that — half a percent"* within a few years. Kiriakou uses the number against the routine deference the courts show to classification stamps: *"maybe 20, maybe 30, maybe 50 — try 95 or 99 and a half"* percent of classified material, in Florence's view, does not merit the stamp.<Cite t="47:00" /><Cite t="47:34" /><Cite t="48:06" />

## The CNN pillow-talk case

On Live on the Fly in November 2021, [John Kiriakou](/wiki/john-kiriakou) said the double standard of espionage prosecution is on display in a 1990s case he witnessed personally at the [CIA](/wiki/cia). A woman he sat next to at Langley was dating a retired senior CIA officer who had gone on to become a CNN talking head; she shared classified information with him as pillow talk, which he then repeated on air. Security called her down, she admitted the disclosure, and she was disciplined with a four-week unpaid suspension and a one-year block on promotion. *"Ever since the Obama administration,"* Kiriakou said, *"that's the very definition of an espionage charge — the [Obama](/wiki/barack-obama) people would have charged her with espionage and certainly the [Trump](/wiki/donald-trump) people would have as well."* He treats the leniency as evidence the classification-and-prosecution system is not about protecting secrets but about selectively punishing dissent.<Cite t="45:14" /><Cite t="45:48" /><Cite t="46:22" />

julian-assange.body_append:
## Why national-security journalists stay silent (2021)

On Live on the Fly with [Randy Credico](/wiki/randy-credico) in November 2021, [John Kiriakou](/wiki/john-kiriakou) laid out the two reasons he believes American national-security journalists have failed to cover [Julian Assange](/wiki/julian-assange)'s prosecution as an existential threat. First, he said, most outlets no longer have a budget for investigative journalism, so they *"crawl into bed with the CIA"* — republishing agency press releases as reporting and, in the case of NBC News's [Ken Dilanian](/wiki/ken-dilanian), literally sending drafts to Langley for clearance before sending them to their own editor. Second, he said, they are afraid. Kiriakou described a Zoom call with attorneys, intellectuals and a handful of journalists at which he watched a Knight Ridder reporter answer a question about his silence on Assange with *"Julian Assange is an activist, not a journalist"* — and, when reminded that Assange was at minimum a publisher, *"you know what, I don't want to talk about Julian Assange."*<Cite t="40:46" /><Cite t="41:21" /><Cite t="42:34" /><Cite t="43:06" />
